To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the equivalence problem for bounded wire delay asynchronous circuits can be solved in polynomial time.

(a) the problem of equivalence checking of asynchronous circuits under bounded wire delay model is reducible to the equivalence checking problem of synchronous circuits, and (b) we give a method to extract the complete flow table of an asynchronous circuit.

the equivalence of the gate-level implementation of an asynchronous design to a given flow table specification can be checked using a product flow table construction, which is a generalization of the product machine construction in the synchronous setting.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the verification of asynchronous circuit designs, with given or measured bounds on wire and delay, with respect to a specification of their behavior, described as a classical asynchronous flow table.
verifying that a given gate-level implementation of an asynchronous system is equivalent to a flow table specification, under bounded wire delays.
the verification of asynchronous circuits with bounded wire and gate delays.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the problem of verifying the equivalence of two asynchronous machines is NP-complete.

the verification procedure described in this dissertation is complete in the following sense: If the initial flow table and the extracted flow table are equivalent, the procedure will detect the equivalence, otherwise, it will detect the non-equivalence.

the proposed method is a practical and effective method to check the equivalence of asynchronous circuit implementations under bounded wire delay model, and is also applicable to asynchronous circuits with multiple clock domains.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that the problem of equivalence checking between a gate-level implementation of an asynchronous machine and the initial specification of the machine is decidable under the bounded wire delays model.
we have developed a complete set of procedures to verify the equivalence of a gate-level implementation of an asynchronous design to its flow table specification.
the product flow table can be constructed in a finite number of steps, and that the product flow is finite and complete.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can verify the equivalence of asynchronous circuits with bounded wire delay models.

the product flow table is a compact representation of the set of possible flow tables, and hence can be used to efficiently check for machine equivalence of the initial flow table with the extracted one.
we can use the classical flow table model of an asynchronous circuit to verify its equivalence under the bounded wire model.
